speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong and I will address Oral Question Nos 1 to 19 and Written Questions 19 to 23 from yesterday's Order Paper, and Question Nos 1 and 2 from today’s Order Paper, as well as a question filed by Mr Seah Kian Peng1 for a future Sitting.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I last updated the House in January this year when we rolled out the national vaccination programme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Globally, we are seeing surges in daily new cases in several countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have also detected several unlinked cases, 10 in the last week.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This suggests that there are unknown cases in our community that caused these infections, which is a cause for concern because, for each unlinked case, there is an unknown source.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For as long as we cannot identify the source, there is a risk that they may be spreading the infection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: New COVID-19 variants have also emerged that challenge our knowledge on the virulence and transmissibility of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To date, we have detected 10 different COVID-19 variants among local and imported cases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A detailed breakdown was shared in MOH’s press release on 4 May.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Such variations in viral strains are not unexpected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is in the nature of viruses to mutate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, we must expect to see new variants emerge from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, some variants are of greater concern because of their increased transmissibility, severity of illness caused or ability to break through vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is also not surprising to discover variant strains in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We cannot completely shut out our borders, close down the causeways, our seaport and airport because Singapore is not self-sufficient in many things and we need to maintain our supply lines and global connections to survive.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The virus will then find ways to infiltrate us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Three of the recent cases at our airport terminals also tested preliminarily positive for B.1.617.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While the definitive characteristics of this variant remain unknown, the large clusters and rapid transmission we see locally are concerning as they suggest that infections of this strain can spread quickly and widely.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is similar to the overseas situation where resurgence of cases is likely driven also by new variants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The emergence of several clusters, new variants as well as the rising number of unlinked cases mean the risk of community transmission has gone up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, we must stay vigilant and tighten our safe distancing measures in the community to slow down and prevent transmission of the virus, even as we make progress in our vaccination programme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have also tightened our border measures to reduce the risk of importing cases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong will elaborate on these shifts in his Statement later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It was a staff nurse who developed acute respiratory infection (ARI) symptoms that day.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: She was immediately tested and, despite the fact that she had completed her vaccination earlier in the year, she was confirmed to be COVID-19 positive.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I should point out that this does not mean that she is the first infected case and had brought COVID-19 into the wards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But her responsible act enabled us to pick up the cluster at TTSH.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our immediate priority in such situations has been to contain and isolate the infections so that they do not spread to the larger community.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Hence, we immediately threw a containment ring around this first detected case, quarantining close contacts and testing everyone who could have been in contact with the individual.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This included all staff and patients of the affected Ward 9D.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: By the next day on 29 April, we had identified three staff and six patients of Ward 9D who were infected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One of these patients had started to display COVID-19-type pneumonia symptoms at this time too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As he had entered Ward 9D earlier on 20 April, testing and quarantine were, hence, further extended to all staff who worked in Ward 9D from 20 April, as well as discharged and current inpatients and visitors to Ward 9D from 20 April.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Testing was also expanded to include all in-patients and all staff working in the main ward block.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: After this first round of testing was completed, all other TTSH staff were also screened.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For additional precaution, patients and staff from the main ward block were also retested a second time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We then threw a larger ring around TTSH, inviting discharged patients and visitors who were in the hospital during the affected period to also be tested.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They are not close contacts and, hence, have a lower risk of infection, but we offered to test them out of an abundance of caution and to give them peace of mind.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For every case detected, a large ring was drawn around them for testing and isolation, and we locked down all wards that had exposure to the infectious cases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is in addition to 12,000 staff, 1,000 patients as well as those who have been quarantined.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to monitor these individuals who have been exposed and retest them where necessary, as some of them may be incubating the infection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They were all either asymptomatic or only exhibited mild symptoms and none of them required oxygen support.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While the numbers are too small to draw firm conclusions, the findings do indicate that vaccination provides critical protection even against COVID-19 variants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We know that while vaccination does not eliminate the risks of infection totally, it does provide significant protection against infections and help to reduce the severity of the disease.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is also likely to reduce onward transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I, therefore, urge everyone to get vaccinated when it is offered to you and continue to comply with safe management measures even if you have been vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will help to keep all of us safe.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: TTSH has implemented a series of measures to prevent further spread within the hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Besides locking down the affected wards, TTSH has also stopped all new admissions to the hospital, restricted visitors and reinforced infection control, hand hygiene and PPE compliance for all staff.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even while we were dealing with the cluster, work was also on-going to understand the source and cause of the infection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Investigation is still on-going and more will be shared when it is ready.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (a) This particular B1.617.2 strain appears very infectious and there will be other variants just like this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (b) Without vaccination, infection among healthcare workers would have been much worse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (c) While vaccine breakthroughs are possible, vaccines can help to prevent severe illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (d) Vaccines can also reduce risk of further transmission, although the extent of which this is true is still being investigated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (e) It is clear that vaccination is most effective when it is part of a whole suite of precautionary measures, such as mask-wearing, safe-distancing, accurate testing, thorough contact tracing, and timely isolation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Since the TTSH cluster happened, there have been reports of healthcare workers there being shunned in public or refused services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I know this comes from a small minority of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The great majority are thankful for the sacrifices and contributions of our healthcare workers, including those from TTSH.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We know you have been working tirelessly in difficult and uncertain conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Despite the stressful situation caused by the outbreak, you continue to do your best to care for our patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I believe I speak for the great majority of Singaporeans, all of us in MOH and everyone in this Chamber, that we are all solidly behind you.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have strengthened our healthcare system, built community care facilities, expanded our testing capacity, enhanced our contact tracing capability, introduced safe-distancing measures and embarked on vaccinating our population, which I will touch on next.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We started COVID-19 vaccinations in Singapore at end 2020 and we continue to make steady progress with our vaccination programme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: About two-thirds of eligible persons aged 45 and above have received the COVID-19 vaccination or booked their vaccination appointments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, we need to continue to encourage more to be vaccinated especially among the seniors, given their age, they are the most vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I urge all of us to encourage our elderly family members too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will be inviting subsequent age bands to receive vaccinations from the latter half of May.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, as vaccine supplies continue to be limited, vaccinations will be progressively extended in smaller age-bands.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If vaccine supplies arrive as scheduled, we will complete the vaccination programme by the end of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We knew from the start that vaccine breakthroughs are possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But vaccination would still significantly reduce the chances of infection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Vaccination also prevents severe reactions to the infections and is likely to reduce onward transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Locally, as of 10 May 2021, 30 local fully vaccinated cases tested positive for COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There were another 24 imported cases that were already vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Most of our local cases of infected vaccinated individuals were asymptomatic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: None had severe COVID-19 disease requiring more intensive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is consistent with the international experience and emerging evidence that vaccines are highly efficacious in protecting against severe COVID-19 disease and likely to reduce the risk of transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There is also a question on re-infected cases, which are known to be possible from overseas and local experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will provide an update when we know more.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Overall, the benefits of the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines continue to outweigh the known risks and we must continue to encourage Singaporeans to be vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One area of concern is the emergence of new COVID-19 variants from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There is intense on-going global scientific evaluation for these variants, which our experts are also participating in.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The current global consensus is that COVID-19 vaccines that have been approved can provide protection against these variants because these vaccines elicit a broad immune response involving a range of antibodies and cells.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to monitor development in this area and assess whether our vaccine programme needs to be adjusted.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Members have also asked about vaccination for children below 16 years old, people with mild allergic reactions and the need for a third booster shot.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The initial data provided by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna at the time of the Pandemic Special Access Route (PSAR) interim authorisation did not include data regarding their use in younger populations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Health Sciences Authority (HSA) has been examining the supplemental data that has since been submitted for the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine to assess if the vaccine meets safety and efficacy requirements for authorisation under PSAR for use in adolescents aged 12 to 15 years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: HSA will also do so for the Moderna vaccine when data is submitted to them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will share more details when the studies are completed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As for children below 12 years of age, clinical trials are still on-going and may take more time before enough data is available.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked if patients who experience mild allergic reactions from the first dose can take their second dose.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Persons who have been assessed by a doctor to be allergic to the first dose of the COVID-19 vaccination are currently contra-indicated from the vaccine and should not continue with the second dose.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We understand that individuals who cannot be vaccinated or cannot complete the vaccination may be concerned that they are not protected from COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These people are kept in our records and we will inform them when there is a suitable vaccine for them or when new evidence that shows that current vaccines can be administered to them is available.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the same time, as more of us are vaccinated, we also protect them indirectly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As for booster shots, data on the need for it is still emerging from both international and local studies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will share more when we know more.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: HSA and the Expert Committee for COVID-19 Vaccinations will continue to monitor on-going studies in areas, such as the extent to which vaccines can prevent onward transmission, the durability of protection provided by vaccines and the effectiveness of vaccines against emerging variants of concern, and will provide updates when available.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Members have asked about adverse effects following vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Only 0.004% of our doses administered had reported serious adverse events.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In general, the observed trend of adverse events within Singapore is consistent with those reported overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The most commonly reported adverse events are not serious.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This includes dizziness, fever, muscle ache, pain at the injection site, headache and allergic reactions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These symptoms generally resolve within a few days.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Most of the patients here have recovered or are recovering from these adverse events.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have also not seen any local cases of unusual blood clots associated with low platelets that have been reported with other vaccines used overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: HSA has released the details of reported adverse events on 6 May 2021, which will continue to be published on a routine basis.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: HSA continues to actively monitor and review the safety of the COVID-19 vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition to monitoring reports from international regulatory counterparts, HSA also reviews reports from local healthcare practitioners on adverse events following vaccination regardless of whether causality can be established.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: HSA has appointed three expert panels to review neurological, cardiac and hypersensitivity adverse events, such as anaphylaxis, which occur following vaccination.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will allow for prompt and appropriate actions to safeguard public health and advance vaccination safety.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked for an update on the Vaccine Injury Financial Assistance Programme, or VIFAP for short.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As of 3 May, 104 applications have been received.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These include 21 cases of hypersensitivity allergic reactions, four neurology-related cases, three cardiology-related cases and one haematology- and dermatology-related case each.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All of them have since been discharged from hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked if we will recognise overseas vaccinations that are not approved by HSA.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Members are aware, the Minister for Transport, Mr Ong Ye Kung, has shared that we are in discussion with several regions on the mutual recognition of vaccination certificates for purposes of travelling.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will release details once arrangements are finalised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A few Members have asked about the progress of the evaluation of Sinovac and other vaccine candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This was how we managed to start our vaccination drive with Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines early.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While there has been a concerted effort to encourage the take-up of COVID-19 vaccinations, such as educating the public on why vaccinations are needed, we are aware of vaccination misinformation too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked what we are doing about this and how we can address this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Overall, public education remains a cornerstone of our vaccination programme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Government agencies have been using multiple platforms, including print and broadcast media, social media, direct messaging platforms and Gov.sg, to communicate essential information about COVID-19, including its vaccines, to all segments of society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All of us have a role to play in stemming the spread of misinformation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Once again, I urge everyone to check that the information they receive comes from reliable sources and make the effort to verify before sharing them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This came at an unfortunate time as I know many Singaporeans are looking forward to the upcoming Hari Raya and Vesak Day celebrations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, the recent community cases show that there remain risks of COVID-19 outbreaks locally and we need to remain vigilant to avoid an uncontrolled resurgence of community cases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I want to thank Singaporeans for your understanding and appeal to everyone to follow the safe distancing measures to prevent further spread of COVID-19 and keep Singapore safe even during these festive seasons.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The past year has been a tumultuous year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One of the biggest challenges was striking a right balance between saving lives while preserving livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But we have built many new capabilities to meet the new challenges as they emerge.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to learn, improve, be nimble in our response and adapt as the situation evolves.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our recovery is contingent on the world's ability to contain the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I want to particularly thank the healthcare professionals – doctors, nurses, allied health – both in the public and private sectors for their support in our public health and medical aspects of our COVID-19 response.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Sometimes, we had to move very quickly and adjust our measures in quick succession, which we know can be very disruptive.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am glad that Singaporeans could come together as a nation, make personal sacrifices to adapt to the new normal and all of us can stand shoulder to shoulder in our fight against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This ability for all of us to strive together is the most critical element in our response to COVID-19 that will make all the difference in the eventual outcome.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Let us continue to work as one and I am sure we will emerge stronger together from this crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: From the start, we have said this is a marathon, not a sprint.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Really, no one knows how long the pandemic will go on for.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Vaccination is a key to ending the pandemic but it will take a very long time to vaccinate the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meanwhile, the virus is not waiting for us.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, there is still a long road ahead of us in this fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do not know how the path of the pandemic will evolve and we must be mentally prepared for a long road ahead with many curveballs and many more twists and turns.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One scenario is that the virus will never go away.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will then have to learn to live with it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At a personal level, this means we try to lead our lives as normally as we can but manage the impact of the virus by getting vaccinated every year and taking sensible precautions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a country and economy, we will then continue to connect with the world to earn a living but we set up strong border defences, establish protocols for safe business travel, partner safe countries to open up our borders and keep hospitalisations and fatalities as low as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are not there yet but we are planning ahead, looking at different scenarios of how the pandemic will unfold and preparing our drawer plans and responses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this journey, we are bound to face some bumps and setbacks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We worked together to overcome some of these difficult challenges last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: After we exited the circuit breaker, we set out a three-phase roadmap to re-open our economy and to resume activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We highlighted then that this re-opening process was not going to be a straightforward one and there would be potential stops and starts along the way because the virus has not been eradicated in our community and new cases can leak through our borders despite our precautions and safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the more we open up and the more activities we undertake, the higher the risks of new cases breaking out in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: How do we manage COVID-19 and protect both lives and livelihoods under these very difficult circumstances?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members – Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Don Wee, Mr Alex Yam, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Leong Mun Wai and Mr Seah Kian Peng – have raised questions about our border measures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One option for us is to shut our borders and minimise the flow of people into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Larger, continental-sized or resource-rich countries like China, Australia and New Zealand have taken this approach.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are able to keep things going with their own resources and people and sustain a living with their own domestic demand.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But Singapore is in a completely different position.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are a little red dot fully plugged into the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For us, these are not just good-to-have; they are existential issues.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are how, as a country, we earn a living and remain relevant to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, we can keep our borders closed for a short time, but not over a prolonged duration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why after we exited the circuit breaker last year, we also progressively lifted our travel restrictions and allowed travellers to come in, but in a controlled and safe manner.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We recognised then that there would be a risk of some imported cases leaking into the community and we had taken several steps to strengthen our precautions and safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, we put in place a system of regular testing for those working at the checkpoints and borders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We prioritised vaccination for them and those working in our Stay-Home Notice (SHN) facilities – the hotels.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We stepped up our testing protocols with pre-departure and on-arrival PCR tests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We tightened our SHN regime and ensured that the hotels we use for SHN have proper infection controls and security measures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also continue to update the SHN regime to respond to the evolving public health situation here and abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some Members have suggested extending the SHN to 21 days.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, we did so initially for the incoming Construction, Marine and Process (CMP) workers, because they would be living and working in higher risk settings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, these workers would serve out 14 days in the SHN facility, followed by seven days in the Migrant Worker Onboarding Centres.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also applied a 21-day SHN for arrivals from the few countries where the variant strains originated: the United Kingdom, South Africa, India.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But these strains are now circulating everywhere in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, it has become increasingly difficult to target just countries where the strains originated.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I should clarify that there is still no medical evidence that the new variants have a longer incubation period.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked if it is possible for vaccinated citizens and PRs who travel abroad to serve their SNH at home.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we will continue to review and consider options for the future, especially as we gain a better understanding of the new variants and when more of our population are vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked about the business travellers who do not need to serve SHN.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have explained before that we allow a small group of such travellers for essential work reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We control the risks tightly by keeping the numbers small and requiring them to adhere strictly to a controlled itinerary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also subject them to frequent testing while they are in Singapore to ensure they are free from the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The scope and usage of such travel passes are subject to constant review and close monitoring to ensure they are used in a safe manner, while minimising risks to the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Importantly, besides the SHN and testing protocols, we control tightly the overall flow of travellers coming into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We adjust the travel flows from each country regularly based on our assessment of the public health situation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Once we observe any deterioration in any country or region, we will throttle down the numbers and impose stricter border restrictions for that country or region.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That was the approach we took recently because of the rapidly deteriorating COVID-19 situation in India.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Pre-COVID-19, we had 200,000 travellers coming through Changi Airport every day, both on transit as well as entering Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This plummeted during the circuit breaker when we closed our borders temporarily.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: After the circuit breaker, as I mentioned, we eased some of our travel restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: By November last year, we had about 820 arrivals a day.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Eight hundred and twenty arrivals a day, compared to 200,000 transit and arrivals.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One reason for the increase in arrivals is that we had taken in more migrant workers for the Construction, Marine and Process (CMP) sectors as well as foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This group was also the largest contributor to our imported cases – they account for about 40% of the imported cases over the recent six months.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But even as we increased the flow of these workers, we also implemented a tighter screening and quarantine process for them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, these imported cases were already in SHN when we detected them and they were not in contact with the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the inflow of CMP workers we have allowed up to now is still unable to meet our needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because every day, every week, every month, many migrant workers have left to go back to their home countries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Whatever numbers we are bringing in barely replace those who have left.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our companies, including many SMEs, urgently need new workers to make up the shortfall and have been applying to MOM for approval to enter Singapore, as you have heard just now in the Parliamentary Question that was posed to Minister Tan See Leng.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The application backlog has been building up significantly, even before we imposed the latest set of travel restrictions on the South Asian region.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I fully understand and share the desire amongst many to be tight on our border measures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we have maintained a tight posture, as I have explained, and we will continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we also need to be very clear what this means for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we can expect many new BTO projects to be delayed by one year or more.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Private home buyers may also face delays of varying lengths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, companies in the marine and process sectors will be badly affected.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They will find it hard to deliver their existing projects on time and a few may even have to forgo new opportunities and projects.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are important sectors that we have taken decades to build.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They hire thousands of Singaporean engineers and executives, and they remain crucial sources of highly skilled jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The manpower shortage will not be confined to the CMP sector; it will have a cascading effect on the whole economy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, any company seeking to bring in workers from higher risk countries will now face considerable delays.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The waiting time for an entry approval could be more than six months.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our big concern is that if companies continue to face difficulties or are forced to close, we could then end up with higher unemployment and job losses for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Stresses will be felt in our society too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singaporeans will find it harder to reunite with their families abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Families applying for new foreign domestic workers to care for their children or elderly will have to wait for at least two months.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are the consequences of keeping our borders tight.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I hope Members will help to explain this to your constituents when you receive appeals, be it to shut down borders completely or to relax the restrictions to allow their workers or foreign domestic workers to come in.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meanwhile, the Government will do more to assist the CMP sector which is bearing the brunt of the impact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The industry has been working very hard to become more manpower-lean.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why MND has set out new legislation to allow existing construction contracts to be adjusted to take into account the increase in manpower costs; we are debating that later.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As announced recently, CMP firms will receive higher Foreign Worker Levy rebates from May to December 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond the CMP sector, as well as the aviation and tourism-related segments, there are signs of improvement in the broader economy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Barring a setback to the global economy and provided we are able to keep the COVID-19 situation under control, we should be able to continue with our recovery trajectory.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But things are very fluid and the outlook remains uncertain.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government will continue to keep a close watch over the economic situation and consider how best to support those who need more help to adjust.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, businesses will also need to be more agile and to start factoring the need to pivot plans or operating models at short notice.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will all need to learn to adapt quickly and be more nimble in this new uncertain and rapidly changing environment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even with the tightest of border controls, there may still be imported cases leaking into the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I shared earlier that countries like China and Australia have adopted a tighter border regime than us because they can afford to rely on a larger base of domestic resources and demand.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But even these countries have detected cases of new variants in their communities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we cannot just rely on border measures to keep out the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also need to have a full suite of protective measures and safeguards in our community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When a new case pops up, we move in quickly to isolate all the close contacts and ring-fence them, as we have been doing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We cast a wide net and conduct mass testing for all persons with possible exposures to the infected case, like what you have seen recently, when we went in quickly to test everyone in the schools or everyone working in the airport.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Thus, we try our best to prevent large clusters and outbreaks from happening.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Despite these efforts, there will be a few occasions when we will need more general movement restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, with the recent Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH) cluster, the transmission was detected some time after the virus was introduced into the ward.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have tested all the hospital staff, patients as well as visitors and tried to ring-fence the cluster.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I recognise that these measures pose considerable inconvenience to all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Minister Gan Kim Yong said just now, there are several public holidays coming up in the month of May.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many activities and plans have had to be adjusted.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I know, in particular, this must be very disappointing for our Malay/Muslim community, having to observe these strict rules during Hari Raya and to curtail your normal family visits for a second year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, for the Buddhist community during Vesak day.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I hope everyone understands why the latest measures are necessary and I thank everyone for taking them in your stride.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I seek your cooperation to abide by them – not just with the letter of the law but also the spirit of it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think it is very important for us to understand that we are now on the knife's edge and our community cases can go either way over the next few weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have a chance of getting things under control by the end of the month.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But, as we know from experience, it only takes one lapse or one irresponsible action for an infection to spread and that infection may end up being a super-spreader event in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, let us all do our part: work from home, cut back on social activities and interactions, and stay home as much as possible during this period.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is not the first time we have had to deal with spikes in community cases.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This puts us in a much safer position.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our experiences over the last year have shown that if we act quickly to contact trace, isolate, test and, if we all exercise individual and social responsibility, we can effectively suppress the spread of the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have brought down infection rates in the community before and we can do it again.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must also continue to support one another.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many have been fighting COVID-19 for more than a year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, our healthcare professionals testing, vaccinating and treating patients; our contact tracing teams; our public officers across multiple Government agencies; our Safe Distancing Ambassadors and Enforcement Officers and many, many more serving on the frontline.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Remember, the virus does not respect ethnicity or nationality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is not a Chinese virus or an Indian variant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must continue to stand together, look out for one another, so that we can all get through this together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am a healthcare worker, with brothers and sisters in the Labour Movement in the Healthcare Services Employees' Union (HSCU).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have got brothers and sisters on the TTSH frontline.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I hear of nurses who have been told by their landlords to move out at short notice.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I know of a young mother of a newborn at home, her husband works at TTSH.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He has had to move out of the home to keep her and her fellow healthcare workers working at another hospital safe from COVID-19 transmission between hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is there a hotline for affected TTSH staff to call?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Ministry set up a care team connecting the different Government agencies to provide help to affected TTSH healthcare workers, especially for challenges that may be beyond the reach of individual hospital management?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I have mentioned my speech, we have observed a minority of our resident Singaporeans taking steps to protect themselves at the expense of our healthcare workers' well-being.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of them have been asked to move out of their homes by their landlords.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are struggling because, on one hand, we know this is wrong and we should not condone such actions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But on the other hand, we are concerned about the well-being of the healthcare workers and we do need to find ways to help them and support them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, MOH and the Multi-Ministry Task Force have been working together with the hospitals – TTSH as well as the other hospitals – to provide support for the affected workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think it is still our preference to encourage our landlords to understand the situation, to play their part to support our healthcare workers in the work that they do.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I also want to urge Singaporeans to show their support to these healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Because they are putting themselves in harm's way in order to protect us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, let us work together to protect them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And, certainly, I think all of us want to thank all the healthcare workers for continuing to protect all of us, given that this COVID-19 pandemic will continue to throw more curve balls at us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have a few supplementary questions for the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Minister Gan has mentioned that the vaccination supplies are limited.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, they are, and very precious at that.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We know that two of them have been certified; Sinovac is being tested.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Do we have arrangements with the other drug companies that can increase the supplies from the other two companies, so that Singaporeans who have not been vaccinated can be assured that they will certainly get that vaccination?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The second supplementary question, I know it is a bit further ahead, but we always like to plan ahead: booster jabs and second jabs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think it is important that every Singaporean and everyone who is working here knows how much we are spending to get all of us safe.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And that leads me to the last question.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong talked about the implications, the overall costs of all this.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think consumers, the public, probably also would have to expect that certain costs will have to go up.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think we just need to be prepared for all these.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Businesses need to absorb, need to find ways to work around some of these.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Government, I am sure, will continue to help subsidise some of these.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I think the public and consumers too need to think about what are the implications for all of us, as all of us are in this together.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Also, partly because there is still a resurgence of new cases every day in many other countries and, therefore, the global supply of vaccines is limited and not just the quantity but the logistics are also challenging.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we need to do what we can to diversify our sources and to ensure that our supplies that we have contracted arrive on schedule.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And when we roll them out, we encourage Singaporeans to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have several other alternatives with which we have entered into advance purchasing agreements.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I am not at liberty to share the details because many of these agreements contain confidentiality clauses that limit us and our ability to share details.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But as and when these contracts materialise, as and when we are able to supply and to deploy these vaccines, we will share more details with fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I have mentioned, let us focus on the current vaccine roll-out.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the end of the day, it may turn out to be similar to the flu jabs that we get every year.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Because of the variants, because of the different virus and bacteria that we are confronting, so we need to continue to have booster jabs for our flu vaccines.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Similarly, for COVID-19, it may come a day that we have to continue to have regular booster jabs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And we are putting in place plans to operationalise that.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In terms of the cost of vaccination, it varies from vaccine to vaccine.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Actually, a significant part of the cost is not in the vaccine Itself but in the logistics of it.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The cost in organising the vaccination centres, mobilising the healthcare professionals, providing support for vaccine recipients; and all these are costly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But if you compare it with the cost of the impact on lives, on livelihoods, I think it is a small price to pay and we need to continue to prepare ourselves and to focus on the vaccination programme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But it is important for us to continue to press on with the vaccination programme to minimise the cost on the economy and the cost of lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The point made by Minister Lawrence Wong about not engaging in xenophobia is something that chimes with me.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was alleged that a Singaporean woman of Indian descent was assaulted by a man who used racial slurs and kicked her for not wearing a mask.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This and another racial incident come in the wake of the community spread, once again, of COVID-19, this time, attributable to a variant coming from the Indian subcontinent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What steps will the Government take to nip this in the bud to address the situation?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The facts we have are as reported in the media.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last Friday, 7 May, in the morning, a 55-year-old Indian lady was brisk walking towards Chua Chu Kang stadium.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She said that she lowered her mask below her nose to prevent breathlessness.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A man wearing a light-coloured t-shirt, accompanied by a woman, shouted at her to put her mask above her nose.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She had scratches on her arms and hands.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She lodged a Police report that night and she said that she would seek medical attention on 10 May – yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The attacker is believed to be a Chinese.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have seen racism around the world during this pandemic: in the US, for example, Asians, particularly Chinese, being attacked; the virus being described as "Chinese virus" or "Wuhan virus", as if viruses have nationality.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Equally, we have to condemn such behaviour in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have said previously there has always been racism in Singapore like in other countries but we have managed it and, over time, we have sought to reduce it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Around the world, economic pressures have led to populism and the populists have been seeking political profit by exploiting people's fears over jobs and economic insecurity, blaming foreigners and blaming immigrants for all of a country's problems.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Singapore, we have avoided the worst of such populism but people are concerned for their jobs, and naturally so.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Amongst Singaporeans, there are legitimate concerns about foreigners taking over our jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The concern is fair and the Government's duty is to protect Singaporean jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But these concerns have been fuelled by unacceptable practices, for example, unfair employment practices that favour hiring foreigners and discriminate against our locals.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a minority who behaves like this, but it naturally makes Singaporeans unhappy.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Anyway, not everyone can distinguish between foreign-born Indians and Singaporean-born Indians.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The lady who was attacked has been a citizen for 25 years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we go down this route, eventually, all Indians can be targets of hate, the so-called "outgroup" which I referred to in a Ministerial Statement a couple of years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not the case now – far from it – but expression of overt racism is still there only amongst a minority in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The majority of Singaporeans are decent and not racist.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But if we continue to fan the flames of racism, we will get to a more uncomfortable position.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are also websites which deliberately fan racism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are anti-Government; that is perfectly okay, but do not play with race.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Comments on these sites – Indians being called cockroaches, rapists and so on – we should be ashamed that in the name of free speech, we allow such comments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This bad behaviour and open expression of racism, I invite all here to condemn.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And when called out, we cannot seek to justify such racist behaviour by saying, "Oh, it is because of Government policies" or "It is because of the India-Singapore Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA)" or that the Indians are behaving badly or that we are entitled to be racist and xenophobic because of these things.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Just ask whether racism and xenophobia can ever be justified on these grounds.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There have been several canards about CECA, promoted by a whispering campaign.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You know that most of what is said about CECA is false.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This morning, a friend of mine overheard in a coffeeshop a conversation among five elderly gentlemen.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They discussed the incident covered in the media of an Indian expatriate family.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not know the facts; several highly racist comments targeting Indians.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is getting into the ground and being repeated.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will become normalised if we are not careful.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I hope responsible Opposition parties will take a stand on this, notwithstanding that many of these sites that promote xenophobia support you.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to make a living by being open to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will fail if we allow racism and xenophobia to become prevalent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is contrary to everything that has made us successful and proud to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In reply to the Minister's comments just now, we are very interested to take up the CECA issue at some point in time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think we still need to understand the situation more, like what the Minister has said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I must state at the outset that the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) and myself are not being xenophobic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are just stating the economic effects some of these free trade agreements have had on our economy – the feedback gathered from many suffering Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We still need to know the situation better but we are definitely not xenophobic and, definitely, racism has no place in our overall thinking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is all about economics, about livelihoods and, today, we are here talking about COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also about livelihoods, about lives over economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sometimes, we may have to give up some of our economic benefits for the sake of lives.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But at the end of the day, we still need to balance and see what is good for our overall livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I will take up the challenge from the Minister – that we will take up this issue at an appropriate time in the future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I just want to confirm that that is correct.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned that if we set the threshold too low, many people will be ruled out from their second dose after reporting allergic reactions and this will impact the overall immunity rate of our country.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When COVID-19 cases were discovered in Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH), the hospital completely stopped accepting new admissions and many patients were diverted to other hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Should cases be uncovered in other hospitals after the mass testing, will they, too, stop accepting new admissions?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If so, the remaining hospitals may get overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am not saying that we should not conduct mass testing, but do all hospitals have a business continuity plan to avoid a complete lockdown if new cases are discovered?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I must say that I am not a doctor.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I cannot give the Member a medical advice here.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: My suggestion is that if you go down to the vaccination centres, there are medical professionals there, they will make an assessment and it will have to be on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But different forms of allergic reaction will have to be assessed by the medical professionals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But generally, if the allergic reaction is mild, you should be able to continue to receive vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we have to be careful because we do want to minimise adverse reactions, particularly those which are more severe.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is a calibration and we will have to leave it to the medical professionals to make an assessment on the ground.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, this is something that we are working on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But it is again important for us to test all our workers at this point in time because we are concerned that similar situations might happen in other hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we do not detect the clusters and cases fast enough, it will become a widespread transmission within the other hospitals and this will be an even bigger problem.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Sometimes, some may say it is better not to know.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But, as far as I am concerned, I think it is better to know than not to know.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At least, if we know that there are cases, we can deal with it, we can implement contingency plans to manage the patients and to also help the healthcare workers in these hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I would urge Singaporeans to also refrain from going to emergency departments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If it is not an emergency case, not an urgent case, then go to our primary care clinics and get your issues attended to.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If it is an emergency, if you are having a stroke or have a heart attack, if you have problems, do go to the emergency departments and we will take care of you.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I want to thank Minister Gan for acknowledging the dutifulness of the staff and all of Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH).

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am married to a TTSH staff and many TTSH families are now made to live apart to reduce risk to other hospitals, to better support the needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But I am concerned about possible on-going community spread.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Would there be a consideration to make it compulsory to swab all patients visiting a hospital, whether inpatient or outpatient?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is something that we are studying but it is not easy to swab all patients because some of them would already have symptoms and some of them may already have pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of them, even after swabbing, could be negative.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They could also be infected by visitors and they could also be within the incubation period and they can become positive thereafter.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is important for us to put in place safe distancing, safe management measures even within the hospital to ensure that precautions are taken.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The staff, healthcare workers must wear the necessary protective wear, whether it is PPE, depending on the setting; even in the inpatient wards or outpatient areas, precautions have to be adopted.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We cannot assume that after swabbing, everyone would be safe.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we are looking at to what extent we can extend the testing for visitors and for patients that are admitted into hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many of my residents and friends who have taken the jab at the vaccination centres, they have had very good experience.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: They said the staff are patient and efficient.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Kudos to the staff at all the vaccination centres in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I have supplementary questions for the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Last but not least, I would like to touch on a point by Dr Tan Wu Meng to say that taxis are shunning the Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare my interest as the ComfortDelGro Taxi CEO.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In fact, a cabby had just texted me that he has been encouraging his fellow cabbies to not shun TTSH.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Each time we pick up an infected case, we are seeing larger clusters.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More people are being infected than, say, the experience last year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, what this means for us is that we really need to take this seriously.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We should take all the safe management measures and all the infection protocols very seriously.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: People who need to wear PPE need to be very diligent about this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those who are in close contact or doing high-risk jobs need to be very diligent about wearing of masks, for example, and make sure they are wearing a proper mask.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are all basic things but I think it is worth re-emphasising.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The other point is that testing can be a big help.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have seen how, through very frequent testing, either by doing a special sweep of everyone or doing it on a regular basis, we are able to pick up cases very quickly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is an important point that we should not give up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Vaccination is important but testing remains an important way for us to detect the virus quickly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When we talk about events that are coming up, certainly, we will apply all of these lessons – infection control, safe-management measures and frequent testing – to ensure that these events can be conducted safely.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have a clarification for the Minister for Health and one for the Minister for Education.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Before I do that, I would just like to assure him that I, too, feel nostalgic that this may be the last time that I would have the chance to pose health-related questions to him after the last 10 years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, the feeling is mutual in that sense.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On to my question, it is about the Vaccine Injury Financial Assistance Programme which he gave some figures on just now.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, for these 75 rejected cases, was there actually an accompanying medical certification that the side effect is related to the vaccination?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And could he clarify why those applications were rejected?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the Minister for Education, the recent round of tightening measures included some that affected the fitness industry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I think he is aware that this has caused a lot of unhappiness and anxiety, as it affects the livelihoods of trainers and also the customers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Subsequently, there was a slight adjustment to this announcement to say that low-intensity activities would be allowed to carry on indoors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If there can be some additional measures, such as requirement to wear gloves and so on, would the Government re-look at this requirement for customers to bring their own equipment to the fitness studio?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am actually interested in the answer to the second question.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of it may be rashes, maybe some swelling, but does not require extensive medical care and, therefore, may not qualify for the application.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But suffice to say that they are all assessed thoroughly by an independent panel before they were approved or rejected.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Last year, Members will recall, Zouk, maybe even now, has been transformed and changed to different kinds of activities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in that sense, we continue to apply the same approach now to gyms and fitness centres.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because we have seen evidence of spread in other places, we have had infected persons use gyms and fitness centres in Singapore, and we have been very worried of large clusters potentially breaking out in these settings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the specific issue of equipment, we will be prepared to look at it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is concern, obviously, because there will be infection, not just through droplets but also fomites and touching the surfaces.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Remember how last year we encouraged everyone not to use your hands to touch your face?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is the reason why we suggested people bring their own equipment, but we will continue to monitor the situation very closely.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will see if there is any possibility of modifications along the way, depending on how the next few days and weeks unfold.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung, you have a clarification?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I thought I would just add more to the answer that the Minister for Education had given to Mr Ang Wei Neng on the lessons learnt for Changi Airport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We know that the sea port and the airport are points of vulnerability when we have a pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in fact, just this morning, we got information that, in Taiwan, their biggest airline has been infiltrated by the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, they are tightening up rules on pilots.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, even for Taiwan, which has kept itself domestically very safe, the virus will find itself through the borders.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Airport, sea port, causeway, these are our points of vulnerabilities, regardless of where the variants and the virus come from.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have been implementing a very tight posture both for sea port and airport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The workers all observe safe management measures, masks on, some are even in full PPE when they carry out their work.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We test them regularly – some on a seven-day cycle, some on a 14-day cycle – which is why we are able to pick up these cases quite quickly this round when we had the outbreak of cases.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thirdly, it is to push them for vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They were one of the first to go for vaccination.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They may come into contact; actually, they do come into contact with travellers, so they are higher risk.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we have taken all these measures, but the mutant virus still found its way through the kink in the armour.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think never be complacent, not even when you are vaccinated; never be complacent.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I put out some information two nights ago, but let me just briefly recap.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first thing when something like that happens is to press the reset button and contain the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Put two rings immediately, that Minister Lawrence Wong and Minister Gan Kim Yong mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First ring, who are the close contacts, quarantine and then isolate.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It should be carried out these few days; started yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Members should expect that, as we do such special operations, we will be picking up cases in the next few days.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, please do expect some cases coming out from the airport because we are doing a very massive one-time sweep.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Beyond that is to put in place greater, more effective segregation measures, so that airport workers who are more risky do not mix with other workers or members of the public.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, places like the canteen and food court, we now do takeaways for them, so that we do not mix them.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thirdly, we continue to do surveillance and the testing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the speed with which we pick up cases is absolutely critical.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And, lastly, push those that have not gone for vaccination to go for vaccination as fast as we can.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just two points of clarification for the Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that the US Food and Drug Administration has just approved the use of the Pfizer vaccine for children aged 12 to 15, and this is just a very recent development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I am wondering, assuming that HSA finds that it is safe to do so, can we assume that we will proceed to vaccinate school-going children above the age of 12 with the vaccines that we have?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My second clarification is on the vaccination effort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think the Minister for Health shared very heartening figures about the progress that we have made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The majority of people over 60 years old have been vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given how key this vaccination effort is to our fight against COVID-19, I am wondering if MOH is studying the example of a handful of countries which have been very successful and made very rapid progress in vaccination – Israel is one example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I believe roughly 90% of those over 60 years old in Israel have been vaccinated in a very short time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are we studying those examples to see what lessons we might be able to learn in order to accelerate the speed of this vaccine roll-out in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
